messages.subject: beginner requests help: censored regression
parts:
For my first stan analysis, I wanted to extend the
censored regression model decribed in the stan_2.9.0
manual, pp. 108-109, to allow for covariates, ie to
implement what econometricians call the tobit model.
This is the model version that does not impute the
censored values.

My stan results are so different from the ML results
using the tobit estimator from the AER package that
I think I must be doing something wrong. (See
particularly the mean of the distribution of beta[2]).
With stan using by default uninformative priors,
one would expect the results to be close, no?

Could I  persuade someone to take a look at this
and see if they can diagnose what's going on?

Thanks!!

##### R session     (results below)
library(rstan)
library(AER)

load("c:/work/limdep/aasho/r/aasho.rdata")

U<-max(rigid25$ltrig)

model<-ltrig~lslabdd+laxles+lwta

# fit the tobit model
(summary(tobit(model,data=rigid25,right=U)))

# now set up the data for stan
id_cens<-rigid25$ltrig==U 
mmx<-model.matrix(model,data=rigid25)
y_obs<-rigid25$ltrig[!id_cens]
x_obs<-mmx[!id_cens,]
x_cens<-mmx[id_cens,]
K<-dim(mmx)[2]
N_obs<-length(y_obs)
N_cens<-sum(id_cens)

# lets recheck tobit using these constructed data
dd<-cbind(y_obs,x_obs)
dd<-rbind(dd,cbind(U,x_cens))
dd<-dd[,c(1,3,4,5)] # remove the intercept column
dd<-data.frame(dd) # convert to data frame
colnames(dd)[1]<-"ltrig" # name of dependent variable

(summary(tobit(model, data=dd,right=U)))
# this agrees with the earlier version

# now for stan: form the data list
data<-list(y_obs=y_obs, x_cens=x_cens, x_obs=x_obs,
                     K=K, N_obs=N_obs, N_cens=N_cens, U=U)

# re-running with iter=10000, warmup=2000
# doesn't change the restults signifcantly                     
fit<-stan(file="aasho2.stan",data=data,
                            iter = 5000 , warmup=1000 , chains = 1 )
print(fit)
get_stanmodel(fit)

messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: Re: beginner requests help: censored regression
parts:
The Stan code from the manual at the bottom of pg. 108 (and top of 109) is just for right censoring so it wouldn't be equivalent to your use of the tobit function, which I think defaults to left censoring at 0. That is, I'm pretty sure the default in AER::tobit is left = 0 so your formula

tobit(model,data=rigid25,right=U)

is really equivalent to 

tobit(model,data=rigid25,right=U, left=0)

If you only want right censoring then I think you need to set left = -Inf.

Hope that helps, 

Jonah

messages.subject: RE: [stan-users] Re: beginner requests help: censored regression
parts:
Thanks you very much!  You’re correct that AER:tobit defaults to left=0, but in my case the actual data meant that specifying left=0 wasn’t needed. As it happens, the tobit results in my note agree with a result in the published literature, so the tobit results aren’t in question.

 

So my real question is: what’s wrong with my stan implementation such that it doesn’t agree with the tobit results? I’m sorry if that wasn’t clear in my original posting.

messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: beginner requests help: censored regression
parts:
Ok I've figured out the issue. It's one of those annoying ones that's so simple but takes a while to actually spot. You just need to get rid of the multiplication by N_cens in the increment_log_prob line. Here's why:

In the example in the Stan manual mu is a scalar parameter so, since there are N_cens censored observations, in the line 

increment_log_prob(N_cens * normal_ccdf_log(U, mu, sigma))

you need the multiplication by N_cens. However, when you go from mu to x_cens * beta you have a vector instead of a scalar and the call to normal_ccdf_log becomes vectorized. The vectorized call to normal_ccdf_log obviates the need to multiply by N_cens since x_cens * beta contains a value for each of the N_cens censored observations. So you just want 

increment_log_prob(normal_ccdf_log(U, x_cens * beta, sigma)) ;

Anyway, when you make that change you should get the correct estimates. 

On another note, I would run at least 4 chains. You also shouldn't need more than the default number of iterations per chain (2000) for a model like this, and you probably don't even need close to that many (I would double check that though).

Best,

Jonah

The reason you want to run multiple chains is to make
sure that diffuse initializations converge to the same
region of the posterior. So it's important to do it
before you do a final run.

- Bob
